extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) and in-house counsel drafting U.S. design patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Practical drafting guidance for preparing U.S. design patent applications focused on maximizing ornamental-appearance protection through figures, line types, claim drafting, continuation practice, and defenses to infringement/validity challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patents protect ornamental appearance, not function
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent protects the ornamental appearance of an article of manufacture (35 USC 171). Functional features are not protectable through design patents - utility patents are the route for functional aspects. The line between ornamental and functional is sometimes contested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the claimed subject matter is ornamental rather than functional. If features are primarily functional, consider a utility patent instead. Be aware the ornamental/functional distinction may be litigated; draft with an eye toward emphasizing aesthetic choices that have alternative functional implementations.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Single Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent has exactly one claim: "The ornamental design for [article], as shown and described." All scope is conveyed by the figures and the explanatory text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft the single claim in the conventional form and rely on figures and description to define scope; do not attempt to add multiple independent design claims. Ensure the descriptive text aligns with and supports the figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Figures Are Everything
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings are the principal means of disclosing the claimed design. Required views typically include: front, rear, top, bottom, left side, right side, and perspective. Each view must be consistent with all others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the full set of required views and ensure consistency across views (no contradictions between views). High-quality, accurate drawings or images are critical because they define the claimed design visually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solid Lines vs. Broken Lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Solid lines depict claimed design features. Broken lines depict unclaimed environmental features (the rest of the product, or context the design is used in).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use broken lines strategically to exclude unclaimed/contextual elements and broaden claim scope; more broken lines generally yield broader scope. Deliberately choose which elements to render in solid vs. broken lines as a primary drafting decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial Designs
rubrics_metrics.description: You can claim part of an article by drawing only that part in solid lines and the rest in broken lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use partial claiming when only a specific feature is novel (e.g., the curve of a phone bezel, the shape of a car grille). This approach is powerful for isolating the novel ornamental feature while excluding the rest of the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple Embodiments per Application
rubrics_metrics.description: A single design patent application can include multiple embodiments only if they are patentably indistinct - usually variations of the same design (e.g., the same shape in different colors). Otherwise file separate applications or use a divisional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether variations are patentably distinct; if not, group them in one application. If variations are distinct, file separate applications or divisional filings to avoid restriction or invalidity issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary Observer Test
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement is determined by whether an ordinary observer would deem the accused design substantially the same as the claimed design (Egyptian Goddess v. Swisa, Fed. Cir. 2008, en banc).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding which features to claim (solid vs broken lines), consider whether those features affect the overall visual impression to an ordinary observer. Draft with an eye toward the visual gestalt that will govern infringement analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functionality Defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Accused infringers often argue the claimed design is dictated by function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To defend against functionality arguments, focus on aspects that have alternative functional implementations and make clear the design choices are aesthetic rather than functionally necessary. Select claimed features and description to emphasize aesthetic motivation where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Spec Discussion of Function
rubrics_metrics.description: In contrast to utility patents, design patent specs say very little. The figures do the work. Avoid discussing function in the spec or describing why the design is the way it is - functionality discussion can support a functionality defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from explaining functional reasons for the design in the specification; such explanations may be used by defendants to argue the design is functional and therefore not protectable as ornamental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation Practice for Design
rubrics_metrics.description: File design continuations to capture additional broken-line strategies as the product evolves and as competitor knockoffs emerge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use continuation filings proactively to pursue different broken-line/claiming strategies over time as products change or competitors design around the original drawings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign Design Protection
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hague Agreement allows international design filings through a single application. Many countries use registered design (not examined) systems with broader scope considerations than US design patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider international filing routes (Hague Agreement or national registered design systems) and be mindful that scope and examination practices differ by jurisdiction; coordinate drawing/claiming strategy accordingly for foreign protection.
